title: The Hermit with the Axe
story:
On the bank of the river Vena stood a great fig tree, and under it the two brothers found a sight that stopped them mid-stride. An old ascetic sat at the root of the tree milking a cow — a cow white as the milky arani tree, her calf beside her, giving milk whenever it was wished. The man himself was white as a flame of fire, dressed in bark with matted locks, worn thin by offering the three sacred oblations day after day, and still as the ocean. Across his shoulder lay an axe.

Krishna recognized him at once, though he had never set eyes on him: Rama, the son of Jamadagni, born in the race of Bhrigu — the one the world called the destroyer of the Kshatriyas. Everything that was said of this man ran through Krishna's greeting: how he had agitated the ocean with the speed of his shafts and laid out the city of Surpara on its shore; how, remembering his slain father, he had gone out with this same axe and cut down the thousand arms of Kartavirya like a forest; how the earth's mud was still said to be stained with the blood of the warrior kings he had slain. The fiercest figure of an older age sat here in the shade of a fig tree, quiet as the preceptor of the gods, milking a cow.

Krishna approached him with respect and addressed him in sweet words. Perhaps, he said, the great sage had heard of two Yadavas living on the bank of the Yamuna. "We are those two." He told him their story without embellishment: from the very beginning of their birth, their father Vasudeva, afraid of Kamsa, had placed them in Vraja, and there they had grown up without fear. When they came of age they entered Mathura and destroyed the haughty Kamsa in the assembly; they set his father Ugrasena back on the royal seat; and then, as before, they returned to the work of cowherd boys. And after all of that, Jarasandha had come against their city, again and again, until the two of them had left Mathura to draw him away.

The old sage listened to the whole of it. This, at last, was a story he understood — the same story he had lived in his own terrible way: the kings of the earth coming against one man, and one man deciding how the kings would fall. And when Krishna fell silent, Parasurama gave his counsel. It was not the counsel of a hermit who counsels peace; it was the counsel of a warrior who had spent his life choosing his ground. Get up, he told them, onto that high summit. If you obstruct Jarasandha by fighting with him from the fort there, you will be able to conquer him. On the heights, where an enemy must climb to reach you, the host of kings would spend itself against stone and against two men who did not tire.

So the mountain was named: Gomanta. The brothers received the counsel as they had received the elders' warning in Mathura — weighing it, turning it, finding the sense of it. It answered the question that had traveled south with them since they left the un-walled city: where, in the end, would the stand be made? Not behind Mathura's missing walls, not on the open road, but on the heights, where a fort could be made of the mountain itself.

They stayed a while with the sage on the bank of the Vena, and when they left, they turned their faces toward Gomanta. Behind them, the old man with the axe went back to his cow, and the river went on past the fig tree, carrying nothing of the war.
reflection: The fiercest hermit in the tradition, who spent his life bringing down warrior kings with his axe, counsels Krishna not destruction but position — the choice of ground. It is an older age handing its wisdom to a new one: the enemy is not to be exterminated but out-thought.
next_story_tease: On the heights of Gomanta, the brothers would find the host of kings waiting — and the sky would open with weapons.
hero_scene: The old sage Parasurama seated at the root of a great fig tree on the bank of the river Vena, axe across his shoulder, milking his white cow, while Krishna and Balarama approach with folded hands through the tall grass.
